narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 57.2% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were your undergraduate GPA, your LSAT score, and your class ranking in the third year of law school. Your LSAT score and third-year ranking were the strongest influences pushing the prediction toward failure, while your undergraduate GPA was the only major factor that slightly pulled in the other direction.

Your LSAT score of 25 sits well below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, and this gap strongly signaled higher risk of struggling with the bar. Similarly, finishing in the second decile of your class in Year 3 (compared to an average around the sixth decile for accepted students) further increased the predicted chance of failure. Although your undergraduate GPA of 3.10 was a bit below the 3.23 average of accepted applicants, it still provided a modest positive signal that helped offset the other concerns somewhat.

Your middle family income and plan to attend full-time were less influential and did not change the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your LSAT score through targeted preparation and strengthening your academic performance in later law school years. Retaking the LSAT and reapplying with a stronger score could meaningfully shift future predictions in your favor. (248 words)
